title: The Overcoat
author: Nikolai Gogol
source: The Collected Tales of Nikolai Gogol (1842) / Translated by Constance Garnett
citation: Gogol, Nikolai. 'The Overcoat.' St. Petersburg Tales, 1842.

sections.heading: The Overcoat (Complete Short Story Selection)

epigraph.quote: Leave me alone! Why do you insult me?

paragraphs: In the department of—but it is better not to name the department. There is nothing more touchy and irritable than departmental officials, clerks, and functionaries of every degree. Suffice it to say that in a certain department served a certain titular councillor, whose name was Akaky Akakievich Bashmachkin. He was a short man, somewhat pockmarked, with reddish hair and weak eyes, who had reached the age of fifty without ever rising above the rank of perpetual copyist.

Akaky Akakievich performed his duties not merely with zeal, but with love. In copying documents he saw an entire, fascinating, varied universe. His favorite letters brought a smile to his lips, and he would wink with his eye and help along with his mouth when his pen was tracing them. Outside this copying nothing seemed to exist for him. He paid no attention to his clothes; his uniform, which had once been green, was now of an indeterminate meal-colored hue, and on his collar there always adhered some piece of straw or thread.

The young clerks laughed at him and made him the butt of their departmental wit, dropping paper scraps upon his bald head and telling him that his landlady was a witch who beat him. But Akaky Akakievich never answered a single word, continuing to copy without making a single slip. Only when the joke became too intolerable, when someone jostled his elbow, did he murmur with pathetic meekness: 'Leave me alone! Why do you insult me?' And in these words there sounded something so pitiful that one young clerk, newly arrived, stopped dead and turned away, feeling as though he had seen the deep tragedy of human misery.

There exists in St. Petersburg a terrible enemy of all who receive a salary of four hundred roubles a year or thereabouts: this enemy is our northern frost. Akaky Akakievich began to feel that his back and shoulders were sorely chilled, for his old overcoat had grown so thin and threadbare that it had lost all warmth, and the clerks called it contemptuously a 'dressing-gown.' He took it to the tailor Petrovich, a one-eyed, drunken artisan who lived on the fourth floor of a dark staircase.

Petrovich examined the coat, turned it inside out, and shook his head: 'No, it's impossible to patch. It's completely rotten; the cloth is like tinder. You must have a new overcoat made.' The words struck Akaky Akakievich like a thunderbolt. A new coat would cost at least eighty roubles! For months Akaky practiced the severest economies: he stopped drinking tea in the evenings, walked on tiptoe over the cobbles so as not to wear out his shoe soles, gave his laundress as little washing as possible, and went without candlelight in his freezing room, sustained by the sublime dream of the new overcoat.

When the coat was finally finished and delivered by Petrovich, it was the proudest day of Akaky's life. The coat was thick, warm, lined with calico, with a collar of fine marten cat. At the department, everyone congratulated him, and an assistant head clerk insisted on hosting an evening party in honor of the coat.

Walking home through the dark, deserted squares of St. Petersburg at midnight after the party, two bearded men in greatcoats suddenly emerged from the shadows. One seized Akaky by the collar: 'That's my overcoat!' and delivered a punch to his jaw, knocking him into the snow. In seconds, they stripped off the magnificent coat and fled into the darkness.

Akaky rushed to the police inspector, and later to a 'Person of Consequence' (a newly appointed general) to beg for aid in recovering his stolen overcoat. But the general, eager to demonstrate his administrative severity, roared at the trembling little clerk: 'Do you know to whom you are speaking?! Do you understand who is before you?!' The terrified Akaky stumbled home through a blizzard, took to his bed with fever, and within three days died of quinsy, leaving behind only a few quills and an old dressing-gown.

Yet soon after his death, terrifying rumors spread throughout St. Petersburg: near the Kalinkin Bridge, a ghost in the shape of a government clerk appeared at night, tearing overcoats from the backs of passers-by, until one freezing night he stopped the carriage of the very 'Person of Consequence' who had terrified him in life, stripped off the general's luxurious beaver coat, and vanished into the fog forever.
